04 / Observation

Tracking the NRHO from Sydney

When can one optical telescope in Sydney actually see a spacecraft near the Moon?

no access

Overview

A telescope sees a spacecraft only when several things are true at once. The spacecraft is above the local horizon. The sky at the site is dark. The spacecraft is lit by the Sun, bright enough to detect, and not lost in the glare of the Moon. This scene applies all of those tests to a Gateway-like spacecraft for one month, with the positions of the Sun and Moon taken from the JPL DE440 ephemeris.

The strip below the scene shows elevation, brightness and separation from the Moon. The green bands are the access windows, the only times a measurement can be taken. An orbit determination filter has to work with these sparse windows and nothing else, which is the problem the estimation part of this work addresses.

What to look for

  1. The access light beside the clock turns green when Sydney can observe the spacecraft.
  2. Around new Moon there are no windows for several nights, because the Moon is up only in daylight.
  3. The gold track in the right hand panel is Sydney carried around by the rotating Earth.

Values from this run

Access windows in 30 days21
Longest window7.4 h
Fraction of the month observable11.3 %
Sky modelJPL DE440
